Neonatal giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) enter the world at a relatively modest size, with newborns typically weighing approximately 1600 grams [Wwb = approximately 1600 grams]. This initial body mass, recorded shortly after parturition, stands in stark contrast to the formidable dimensions the animals attain as adults. A fully grown individual can achieve a total length from the tip of the snout to the end of the tail of about 190 centimeters [Li = about 190 centimeters], a figure that underscores the species’ status as the largest of the extant anteaters. The body itself accounts for roughly 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters] of that measurement, while the bushy, flag-like tail contributes an additional 60 to 90 centimeters [Li = 60 to 90 centimeters]. This substantial appendage serves multiple functions, including thermoregulation and use as a blanket during rest. The dramatic increase in mass from the neonatal stage to adulthood represents one of the most pronounced growth trajectories among xenarthrans, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes rapid early development within the constraints of a low metabolic rate.

Reproduction in the giant anteater is characterized by a notably low intrinsic rate of increase, a direct consequence of extended parental investment and a protracted developmental schedule. At a stable thermal condition of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], females typically give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and produce approximately 1.2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.2 litters per year] under captive settings, reflecting a low fecundity that is typical of large-bodied placental mammals. A successful pregnancy, following internal fertilisation and a period of embryogenesis, culminates in the birth of a single pup; twinning is exceptionally rare. The gestation period itself, during which the foetus develops within the uterus, lasts for 184 days [tg = 184 days], a duration that is comparable to that of other large xenarthrans and contributes to the extended inter-birth interval observed in this species at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C].

The female giant anteater carries the developing young for a period of 184 days [tg = 184 days] before parturition gives way to a single, altricial neonate entirely dependent on maternal care at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. A critical milestone in the early life of the pup is the cessation of lactation and the transition to independent foraging, a process known as weaning. Under captive conditions maintained at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], this dietary transition, marking the end of the suckling stage, occurs approximately 56 days after birth [tx = approximately 56 days after birth]. At this point, the juvenile begins to consume a diet of insects, mimicking the adult's myrmecophagous habits, though it may continue to associate closely with its mother for several additional months. The relatively short weaning period for a mammal of this ultimate size may be an adaptation that allows the mother to reduce the energetic burden of lactation and prepare her physiological condition for a subsequent reproductive event, especially in seasonal environments where prey abundance fluctuates.

The protracted developmental trajectory of the giant anteater extends well beyond the initial weaning event. After achieving nutritional independence, the juvenile enters a prolonged sub-adult phase during which it must accumulate substantial body mass and develop the physiological capacity for reproduction. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 1186 days since birth [tp = 1186 days since birth] in captive settings, a value equivalent to approximately 3.25 years at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This falls comfortably within the broad range of 2.5 to 4 years since birth (2.5-4 years since birth) [tp = 2.5-4 years since birth] reported from field studies in the Brazilian cerrado and the Argentine Gran Chaco at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. The onset of sexual maturity is not solely a function of age but is also tightly linked to the attainment of a critical body size. Adult individuals exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate wet weight; males typically reach an adult body mass of 33 to 41 kilograms [Wwi = of 33 to 41 kilograms], while females are smaller, ranging from 27 to 39 kilograms (27-39 kilograms) [Wwi = 27-39 kilograms].

An understanding of the species' maximum lifespan is essential for contextualizing its slow life history. Under the stable, predator-free conditions of zoological institutions maintained at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], giant anteaters have been documented to survive for up to 31 years [am = up to 31 years]. This considerable longevity, which surpasses the records for most other xenarthrans of similar body mass, is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, low fecundity, and high maternal investment. The achievement of an ultimate wet weight of up to 41 kilograms [Wwi = 41 kilograms] in males and 39 kilograms [Wwi = 39 kilograms] in females requires years of sustained growth, and the extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive opportunities across a female's lifetime. In their natural habitat, however, mortality rates are significantly higher due to predation, habitat fragmentation, and road kills, meaning that wild individuals rarely approach this physiological maximum. The combination of a single offspring per litter and an infrequent breeding schedule makes this species particularly vulnerable to population declines when adult survival is compromised.
